title: Sikhs in science
hookLine: Sikh scientists and doctors have served worldwide, like Narinder Singh Kapany in fiber optics

lines: CAN LIGHT GO AROUND A BEND?
cards: Under the street outside, or under the ocean, a pulse of light is racing along a strand of glass thinner than a hair. It bends around corners and follows the cable down hills and across seabeds.

Your last video call, the photo you sent this morning: there's a fair chance some of it traveled as light inside glass. Long before anyone streamed anything, a young Sikh physicist was asking a simple question.
Can light be made to go around a bend? Today: Sikhs in science.

teach.h: CAN LIGHT GO AROUND A BEND?
teach.b: First, the question. Light, as school science teaches, travels in straight lines.
Narinder Singh Kapany, a physicist from Punjab, worked with others on bundles of very thin glass fibers that could carry light, and even an image, along a curved path.
He wrote about the work under a plain name: fiber optics. Second, how it works.

teach.h: IT BOUNCES BACK IN, AGAIN AND AGAIN.
teach.b: Inside a clear glass fiber, light hits the wall at a shallow angle and bounces back in, again and again, so it stays trapped and follows the fiber wherever it bends. Physicists call it total internal reflection.
The light doesn't go around the corner so much as ricochet around it. Third, the wider picture.

Kapany is one Sikh name in science; other Sikhs have worked as scientists, engineers and doctors, in Punjab and far from it. He also gave his time and money to Sikh art and Sikh studies, and wore the turban.
Science and the Sikh story sat in the same life without a fight. Fourth, the root.

teach.h: THE WORLD WELLS UP FROM ONE LIGHT.
teach.b: At Ang 1349 of the Guru Granth Sahib, in a hymn of Bhagat Kabir, the whole world wells up from one light. Gurbani talks often about jot, the divine light in every being.

A physicist studies how light moves through glass; a Sikh hears of one light moving through every life. Those are different kinds of claim, and nobody needs to blend them. But both start by paying attention to light.

how: Sikhs work in science, engineering and medicine around the world; gurbani speaks of jot, the one light in every being, which Sikhs understand as a spiritual teaching rather than a scientific one.

games.q: you're a young physicist, and everyone says light travels in straight lines. what do you do?
o: accept it and work on something else.
ask whether light can be made to follow a bend in glass.
try to bend light with magnets.
games.why: Kapany, building on earlier experiments by others, worked on fibers that carry light and images along a curved path, and wrote about it as fiber optics.

practice: Sit facing a window or a lamp, look at the light for one breath, then close your eyes and notice the glow that stays behind your eyelids. Let your attention rest on that faint brightness for a while.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru and hold the thought of one light in every being.
